title: Coolcations: Why Travellers Are Swapping Hot Summers for Cold Destinations
metaDescription: Coolcations are the fastest-growing summer travel trend — northern destinations chosen for mild weather. Where to go, when, and what it costs.
excerpt: Mediterranean summers now regularly break 40°C. A growing number of travellers are heading north instead, and the destinations are better for it.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
For most of the last fifty years, the European summer had one direction: south. Beaches, heat, and a tan to prove you went.

That assumption is breaking. Southern Europe now regularly sees July and August temperatures that make sightseeing genuinely unpleasant and occasionally unsafe, and travellers have responded by inverting the map. The industry has landed on the word **coolcation** — a summer holiday chosen specifically for mild weather.

It sounds like a marketing term, and it is. The underlying shift is real.

## What Is Driving It?

Three things at once.

**Heat.** Southern European summers have become reliably hot in a way that changes what a holiday feels like. Walking a city between noon and 5pm stops being an option. Beach days get displaced to dawn and dusk.

**Crowds.** Peak Mediterranean season has become a queueing experience. Venice, Dubrovnik, Santorini and Barcelona in August involve a substantial share of your day waiting.

**Price.** The southern peak is the most expensive travel period in Europe. Northern destinations in the same weeks are having their own peak, but from a lower base and with far more capacity relative to demand.

The result is that a Norwegian or Scottish July increasingly beats a Greek one on comfort, crowding and often cost.

![Summer Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1551801841-ecad875a5142?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Where to Go

**Norway.** The obvious flagship. Fjord country in July sits comfortably in the high teens and low twenties Celsius, with near-endless daylight above the Arctic Circle. Bergen to the Lofoten Islands is the classic route. Expensive — Norway always is — but the daylight effectively gives you 18-hour days, which changes the value calculation.

**Iceland.** Summer is its accessible season: the highland roads open, the puffins arrive, and it barely gets dark. Temperatures rarely exceed 15°C. Book accommodation far ahead; Iceland's capacity is genuinely limited.

**Scotland and the Hebrides.** The best-value coolcation in Western Europe. Long summer evenings, dramatic coastline, and a food scene that has quietly become excellent. Bring midge repellent for the west coast in July and August; this is not optional advice.

**Finland and Swedish Lapland.** Lakes, forest, cabins, saunas, and a culture built entirely around the short summer. Comfortable temperatures, and the midnight sun in the north.

**The Faroe Islands.** Rapidly rising in popularity and still uncrowded. Cool, frequently misty, spectacular. Weather here is genuinely changeable — plan loosely.

**Greenland.** The most extreme option and increasingly accessible, with expanded flight connections. Icebergs, hiking and a short, intense summer.

**The Baltics — Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania.** Pleasantly warm rather than cold, with beautifully preserved old towns, Baltic beaches, and costs well below Western Europe.

**The Alps in summer.** Switzerland, Austria and the Dolomites at altitude. Hiking, lakes, cable cars, and temperatures fifteen degrees below the valley floor. Mountain villages in July are one of Europe's great underrated summer experiences.

![Summer Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1472502516535-eeee381bb45e?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Beyond Europe

**Patagonia and New Zealand** — the southern hemisphere's winter, which is mild in both, and genuinely quiet
**Canada — British Columbia, Alberta, Nova Scotia** — summer highs in the low twenties with the Rockies and coastline at their best
**Japan's Hokkaido** — the reason Japanese travellers head north in August. Lavender fields, cool evenings, excellent food
**Tasmania and southern Chile** — remote, cool, and increasingly on the radar
**The Himalaya** — Ladakh, Spiti and Kashmir during the Indian summer, where altitude does what latitude does elsewhere

## What Does a Coolcation Actually Cost?

Northern Europe carries a reputation for expense that is only partly deserved.

- **Norway and Iceland** are genuinely expensive — budget comparably to Switzerland. Self-catering and supermarket lunches make an enormous difference
- **Scotland, Finland and the Baltics** are moderate, and the Baltics are outright good value
- **Canada and Hokkaido** sit in the middle

The saving that surprises people is **time**. Long daylight means you can do a full day's activity after dinner. A Norwegian summer day genuinely holds more than a Mediterranean one, where the middle five hours are written off to heat.

## What to Pack

The single biggest mistake is packing for the temperature rather than for the variability.

- **Layers, not warmth.** A cool-climate summer day can run from 9°C at dawn to 22°C at midday
- **A proper waterproof shell.** Not water-resistant. In Scotland, the Faroes and Iceland it will rain, and it will rain sideways
- **Waterproof footwear** with grip
- **A warm layer for evenings**, even in July
- **Sunglasses and sunscreen.** Counter-intuitive, and necessary — long daylight at high latitude burns people who assumed cold meant safe
- **An eye mask.** Twenty hours of daylight is wonderful until you try to sleep
- **Insect repellent** for Scotland, Scandinavia and Canada in mid-summer

## The Honest Trade-offs

You are giving up guaranteed weather. A Greek July is hot and sunny essentially every day. A Scottish July is glorious, grey or both within an afternoon.

Two ways to handle this:

1. **Choose destinations where bad weather is still good.** A rainy day in Edinburgh, Helsinki or Reykjavik is fine. A rainy day in a remote fjord cabin with no plan is long.
2. **Plan loosely.** Keep two or three activities in reserve and pick by the forecast each morning rather than locking a schedule a week ahead.

You are also giving up the beach, mostly. Baltic and Scottish beaches are beautiful and cold. If lying in the sun is the point of your holiday, a coolcation is not a substitute — it is a different thing.

## Is It Worth Booking Early?

More than for southern Europe, and for a specific reason: **northern destinations have limited capacity.** Iceland, the Faroes, Lofoten and the Scottish islands have a finite number of beds, and their summer is short. The good accommodation goes six to nine months ahead.

Rental cars sell out entirely in Iceland and Norway in peak summer. If your trip depends on driving, book the car before the flights.

For groups, that capacity constraint is the whole game — a six-person cabin in Lofoten in July is a genuinely scarce object. Agreeing dates fast matters more than agreeing them perfectly. Putting the options in one shared plan on **Trypinn** and settling the week in a day or two, rather than a month of messages, is usually the difference between the trip you wanted and the trip that was still available.
